nameStory: Bur Parsley gets its name from its distinctive fruits, which are covered in tiny hooked spines that stick to clothing and animal fur like miniature burrs. The "parsley" part comes from its feathery, divided leaves that resemble those of garden parsley, though this plant is quite different from the herb you'd find in your kitchen.
description: Bur Parsley is a delicate annual herb in the carrot family that sends up thin, hollow stems topped with small clusters of white flowers. The light green leaves are finely divided and triangular in overall shape, giving the plant a lacy, delicate appearance. It's a relatively small plant, typically reaching 1-2 feet tall, and is quite rare in New England with only a handful of recorded sightings.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The tiny fruits are covered in hooked spines that feel rough and catch on fabric when you brush against them - these burr-like seeds are the plant's calling card

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers arranged in loose, open clusters (umbels) that look like tiny umbrellas - much sparser than the dense flower heads of related plants

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, light green leaves divided into many small leaflets with a triangular overall outline - they feel delicate and tear easily when handled

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, hollow stems that feel brittle and snap cleanly when bent - the whole plant has an airy, delicate structure

habitat: Bur Parsley prefers disturbed soils in open areas like roadsides, field edges, and waste places. It tends to grow in relatively dry, well-drained soils and can tolerate poor growing conditions. Given its extreme rarity in New England, it's most likely to be encountered as a chance introduction near ports or transportation corridors.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic finely-divided leaves, starting as small rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and produce their small white flower clusters, which are most visible from late spring through mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive spiny fruits mature and become most noticeable as they stick to clothing and fur - this is often when the plant is first noticed.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving no above-ground parts to find.

funFact: Despite being in the same genus as Garden Chervil, a popular culinary herb, Bur Parsley is so rare in New England that you're more likely to spot a moose in downtown Boston than find this little plant growing wild!
confusionNotes: Bur Parsley can be confused with other white-flowered members of the carrot family, but the spiny, burr-like fruits are unique - if the seeds stick to your clothes like Velcro, you've found your plant. Remember: "Burrs that stick, that's the trick."
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with Garden Chervil, the cooking herb - while they're closely related, Garden Chervil has smooth fruits without the hooked spines. Also, like many carrot family plants, it's best not to taste any wild specimens as the family includes some toxic species.
compareHints: Bur Parsley differs from its cousin Cow Parsley by being much smaller and more delicate, with sparser flower clusters and most notably, those distinctive spiny fruits. Garden Chervil looks very similar in leaf and flower, but has smooth, elongated fruits without any spines - the burr-like seeds are Bur Parsley's unique signature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cow parsley is much taller and more robust than its relatives bur parsley and garden chervil.
Garden chervil is much more delicate and refined than its wild relatives cow parsley and bur parsley, with softer, more finely-cut leaves and a sweet fragrance.
